questions.q: Name the three main chemical layers of Earth's interior in order from surface to centre, and state the approximate thickness of each.
questions.a: Crust (5-70 km), Mantle (~2,900 km thick), Core (~3,470 km radius). A wrong answer (e.g., listing "lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere") reveals confusion between chemical layers (crust/mantle/core) and mechanical layers (lithosphere/asthenosphere) — a common Class 9 error when students mix plate tectonics terminology with basic structure.

questions.q: Explain why the continental crust is thicker but less dense than oceanic crust, and how this relates to the principle of isostasy.
questions.a: Continental crust (avg. 35 km, density 2.7 g/cm³) is granitic and buoyant; oceanic crust (avg. 7 km, density 3.0 g/cm³) is basaltic and denser. Isostasy means crustal blocks float on the ductile mantle like icebergs — thicker continental crust has deeper "roots" to maintain gravitational equilibrium. A wrong answer focusing only on rock types without mentioning buoyancy/floatation shows misunderstanding of isostasy as a dynamic equilibrium process.

questions.q: An earthquake occurs at 20°N, 80°E. A seismometer at 40°N, 80°E (same longitude, 2,200 km away) records both P and S waves. Another at 60°S, 80°E (angular distance ~100°) records P-waves but NO S-waves. What does this tell you about the state of the outer core? Show your reasoning.
questions.a: Step 1: S-waves cannot travel through liquids. Step 2: At 100° angular distance, rays penetrate the outer core. Step 3: Absence of S-waves at 100° but presence at 20° proves the outer core is liquid. Step 4: P-waves are recorded at both because they travel through solids and liquids. Step 5: This matches the S-wave shadow zone (103°-143°). A wrong answer claiming the mantle is liquid reveals the classic misconception that "mantle = magma".

questions.q: Compare the temperature gradient in the crust (approx. 25-30°C/km) with the mantle (approx. 0.5-1°C/km). Why is the gradient much steeper in the crust despite the mantle being hotter overall?
questions.a: Crust transfers heat primarily by conduction (slow, steep gradient); mantle transfers heat by convection (solid-state creep, efficient, gentle gradient). The mantle's adiabatic gradient is low because rising material expands and cools without losing heat. A wrong answer attributing the difference to "mantle is closer to core" ignores heat transfer mechanisms — a physics-geography integration error.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "The inner core is solid because it is cooler than the outer core." Provide evidence for your judgment.
questions.a: False. Inner core (≈5,400°C) is hotter than outer core (≈4,400°C). It is solid due to immense pressure (≈3.6 million atm) raising the melting point of iron-nickel alloy above the actual temperature. Pressure effect dominates over temperature. A wrong answer accepting the statement shows confusion between temperature and phase diagrams — students must understand pressure melting point relationships.

questions.q: Create a labeled cross-section diagram of Earth's interior to scale (1 cm = 1,000 km) showing all layers with their thicknesses, compositions, and physical states. Include a key explaining how seismic wave paths prove the liquid outer core.
questions.a: A good answer: Diagram with crust (0.005-0.07 cm), mantle (2.9 cm), outer core (2.2 cm), inner core (1.2 cm radius). Labels: Crust (granite/basalt, solid), Mantle (peridotite, solid but ductile), Outer Core (Fe-Ni, liquid), Inner Core (Fe-Ni, solid). Key shows S-wave shadow zone (103°-143°) and P-wave refraction at core-mantle boundary. A poor answer draws equal-thickness layers or labels mantle as "magma" — reveals lack of scale sense and the liquid mantle misconception.
